newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh letter calls for action against "bastards".
newsitem.headline: McVeigh letter calls for action against "bastards".

text.p: Accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh suffered a double blow on Thursday as a witness placed him in the type of truck used in the bombing and an anti-government letter he wrote vowing "to rip the bastards heads off" was entered into evidence.

McVeigh sat impassively as prosecutor Larry Mackey read the jury a letter the 29-year-old Gulf War veteran wrote to a Michigan woman two months before a Ryder rental truck filled with explosives blew up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.

In the letter, McVeigh called himself an "animal," said he wanted to take action and boasted to the woman, "Rip the bastards' heads off, s--- down their necks and I will show you how with a simple pocket knife."
McVeigh was equally impasssive when a motel clerk testified he saw him in a rented Ryder truck between April 16 and 18 at the Dreamland Motel in Junction City, Kansas.
Junction City is a five-hour drive from Oklahoma City and prosecutors said the Ryder truck, which carried the bomb and was destroyed in the explosion, was rented at an auto body shop there.

The clerk, Eric McGowan, 19, said he could not recall exactly which day he saw McVeigh in the truck but distinctly recalled the incident because he had to ask him to move the vehicle because it was blocking another guest's door.

Defence attorney Stephan Jones immediately lashed into McGowan, hinting that he was after a $2 million reward for the capture of the bomber and that he had frequently changed his story -- perhaps to accommodate the government and a horde of reporters eager to interview him.

"You know there is a $2 million reward don't you ... you know I don't have anything to do with who gets that reward, do I?" Jones demanded of McGowan who was 17 when McVeigh stayed at the motel owned by his mother.

The two sparred for 20 minutes over exactly when McGowan had seen McVeigh in the truck -- on a Sunday or a Monday, the day the government says McVeigh rented it. Jones insisted that McGowan had said in interviews he had seen McVeigh in the truck on a Sunday, thus blowing a hole in the prosecution's timeline.

Before McGowan testified, the highlight of the day was testimony about the letter that was written to Gwenn Strider. She was so disturbed by it that she gave it to McVeigh's former roommate, Kevin Nicholas.
He identified the handwriting as McVeigh's and testified that when McVeigh stayed with him he told him not to worry about the long distance calls he was making because he had a pre-paid calling card.
The government maintains that the card was used to shop for components to make the bomb and rent the truck.
In the letter, McVeigh said his body was wearing out possibly because of his Gulf War service and "I might as well do something good while I can still be 100 percent effective.
"My whole mindset has shifted from the intellectual to the animal ... You only live once and it is better to burn out than to rot away in some nursing home."

He asked Strider if she wanted to be put in touch with people who could get her into the militia movement even though her name could wind up on a "super-computer" in Belgium where the names of 300,000 subversives are kept.

The prosecution contends that McVeigh was so upset by the 1993 government confrontation with the Branch Davidian religious cult in Waco, Texas, and a previous shoot-out with right-wing militant Randy Weaver, that he decided to take direct action and blow up the Murrah building.
McVeigh has pleaded not guilty and his lawyers said the government has arrested the wrong man. McVeigh's alleged co-conspirator, Army buddy Terry Nichols, will be tried later.
